### Abstract
Plant-derived monoterpenoid α-terpineol has gained significant attention due to its versatile applications in the food, cosmetic and pharmaceutical industries. Microbial biosynthesis offers an environmentally sustainable approach for its commercial-scale production. Here, we developed a combinatorial engineering strategy to enhance α-terpineol production in Saccharomyces cerevisiae . A truncated Vitis vinifera α-terpineol synthase (tVvTS) was optimized through alanine scanning, site-directed mutagenesis, and N-terminal truncation, yielding a variant with improved whole-cell production performance, tVvTS M522K/13aa , which increased α-terpineol titer by 4.8-fold. Further enhancement of mevalonate pathway flux through enzyme fusion and mitochondrial compartmentalization increased the titer by 26.3-fold relative to the parental strain. Subsequent optimization of tolerance-associated genes expression, diploid construction, and fed-batch fermentation enabled the final strain WB11 to produce 81.78 mg/L α-terpineol in a 5-L bioreactor. This study provides an efficient combinatorial strategy for microbial production of natural terpene alcohols.

### 1. Introduction
α-Terpineol is a valuable monoterpenoid widely used in the flavor, fragrance, pharmaceutical, and cosmetic industries because of its pleasant aroma and diverse bioactivities [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. At present, α-terpineol is mainly obtained from plant extraction, which is constrained by seasonal variation, low recovery, and environmental concerns. Chemical synthesis is feasible but often requires toxic solvents and harsh reaction conditions. Therefore, microbial production has emerged as a promising alternative for the sustainable manufacture of α-terpineol and other “natural” terpenoids [ 7 , 8 ].
In microorganisms, α-terpineol is synthesized from geranyl diphosphate (GPP), which is derived from the native isoprenoid pathway [ 9 ]. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae , expression of a truncated α-terpineol synthase from Vitis vinifera (tVvTS), together with pathway engineering of the mevalonate pathway, enabled de novo α-terpineol production, but the reported titers remained low (3.32 mg/L in shake flasks and 21.88 mg/L in a 5-L bioreactor) [ 10 ]. These results indicate that microbial α-terpineol biosynthesis is still far from industrially relevant levels. Three major unresolved bottlenecks appear to limit this process: the low catalytic efficiency and poor heterologous performance of plant-derived VvTS/tVvTS in yeast, severe competition for the common precursor GPP with endogenous sterol biosynthesis, and the cytotoxicity of α-terpineol that impairs cell growth and production [ 11 , 12 ].
Plant-derived terpene synthases often exhibit low catalytic efficiency and poor performance in heterologous hosts [ 13 , 14 ], making enzyme optimization a key strategy for improving monoterpene production. For example, structure-guided protein engineering has been successfully applied to enhance the activities of geraniol synthase and borneol synthase, leading to markedly improved product titers in microbial hosts [ 15 , 16 ]. However, such strategies have not yet been a

### 2.6. α-Terpineol extraction, identification, and quantification
After fermentation of S. cerevisiae strains, 2 mL of the upper organic phase was transferred to a 2 mL Eppendorf (EP) tube and centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 10 min. The clear upper organic phase was carefully aspirated (to avoid impurities) into a clean 2 mL EP tube and recentrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 5 min. The organic phase was extracted using a 1 mL syringe and filtered through a 0.22 μm organic membrane. The clear filtrate was transferred to an HPLC vial insert and analyzed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) on the same day.

### 2.7. Optimization of medium components
In YPD medium, glucose serves as the primary carbon source, whereas yeast extract and peptone serve as the main nitrogen sources. The calculation formula for C/N is as follows:
C / N = C ( g l u c o s e ) N ( y e a s t e x t r a c t + p e p t o n e ) = X 180.156 g · m o l − 1 × 6 ( 10.9 % × Y + 15.4 % × Z ) 14 g · m o l − 1
where X, Y, and Z represent the concentrations (g/L) of glucose, yeast extract, and peptone, respectively. The molecular weight of glucose was taken as 180.156 g/mol, and each glucose molecule contained six carbon atoms. The total nitrogen contents of yeast extract and peptone were assumed to be 10.9% and 15.4%, respectively. The atomic weight of nitrogen was taken as 14 g/mol.

### 3.1. Structure-guided engineering of tVvTS for enhanced α-terpineol production
We introduced tVvTS (N-terminal 28-amino-acid signal peptide removed) [ 10 ] into S . cerevisiae BY4742 to generate strain WB01. Fermentation of WB01 confirmed that tVvTS is functional in α-terpineol biosynthesis ( Fig. S1 ). However, the initial titer was low, reaching only 0.05 mg/L ( Fig. 1 B). To overcome the low apparent in vivo performance of heterologous terpene synthases, a semi-rational design approach was employed. Due to the absence of a crystallographic structure for VvTS, we constructed a high-confidence homology model using SWISS-MODEL. The resulting model exhibited 55.91% sequence identity and a GMQE score of 0.82, suggesting high reliability. We preprocessed the tVvTS protein and GPP as the ligand using AutoDock software, then performed molecular docking with AutoDock Vina and visualized the best docking pose using PyMOL.
Modeling of truncated α-terpineol synthase from Vitis vinifera (tVvTS) and assessment of α-terpineol production in tVvTS mutants. (A) Molecular docking model of tVvTS with GPP, generated with PyMOL, highlighting amino acid residues within 4 Å of the ligand as identified by docking. (B) α-Terpineol production of tVvTS alanine scanning mutants, targeting residues within 4 Å. (C) α-Terpineol production of tVvTS saturation mutants at six identified key positions: K90, Q127, P215, V288, F290, and M522. All data represent the mean ± standard deviation of three biologically independent samples. Key amino acid residues critical for enzyme function are typically located in or near the binding pocket [ 20 , 21 ]. We thus identified potential key residues as those within 4 Å of the tVvTS ligand-binding pocket. From the docking pose, we selected amino acid residues in the substrate binding site, binding pocket entrance, and other related regions for further characterization ( Fig. 1 A). The identified residues were Q81, Y86, K90, Q127, H128, L210, P215, V288, F290, Y294, S448, I451, I520, M522, and M527. We engineered tVvTS by mutating these re

### 3.2. Strengthening precursor supply improves α-terpineol production
HMG-CoA reductase is a rate-limiting enzyme in terpenoid biosynthesis [ 22 ], and expressing its truncated variant (tHMG1) has been shown to improve terpenoid production [ 23 ]. To boost α-terpineol precursor supply, we expressed tHMG1 in yeast to redirect metabolic flux toward terpenoid synthesis ( Fig. 3 A). GPP is the direct precursor of α-terpineol and an intermediate in farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) synthesis catalyzed by Erg20. Erg20 has a higher affinity for GPP than tVvTS M522K/13aa , thereby limiting tVvTS M522K/13aa apparent in vivo performance. To mitigate Erg20-mediated GPP consumption and ensure sufficient precursor for monoterpenoid synthase, we engineered the Erg20 F96W/N127W mutant (with reduced GPP affinity) [ 24 , 25 ]. Spatial proximity of consecutive enzymes in metabolic pathways facilitates substrate channeling and enhances flux efficiency [ 26 , 27 ]. We thus investigated whether fusing ERG20 F96W/N127W with tVvTS M522K/13aa would improve α-terpineol production. The fusion strategy was designed to potentially promote more efficient intermediate transfer between the GPP-generating enzyme (ERG20 F96W/N127W ) and the GPP-consuming α-terpineol synthase, thereby reducing cytoplasmic diffusion and competitive consumption of GPP by endogenous pathways. Prior studies in S. cerevisiae have shown that fusion expression can, in some cases, outperform separate co-expression for monoterpenoid production. We fused ERG20 F96W/N127W to the N-terminus and C-terminus of tVvTS M522K/13aa via linkers (GS) 5 , respectively. These fusion constructs were integrated into the multi-copy rDNA locus of the BY4742 genome to generate strains WB03 and WB04 ( Fig. 3 A). These strategies collectively improved α-terpineol production. Strain WB04 showed a more pronounced increase in α-terpineol titer, reaching 0.84 mg/L. This titer was 3.5-fold higher than that of the parental strain WB02 ( Fig. 3 B). Notably, this 3.5-fold titer improvement is consistent with a possible benefit

### 3.3. Redirecting GPP flux toward α-terpineol biosynthesis
Endogenous Erg20 in yeast converts GPP to FPP, which limits α-terpineol production. To maximize α-terpineol production, we targeted deletion of the endogenous ERG20 gene. We integrated the ERG20 F96W/N127W and tVvT SM522K/13aa fusion protein into the ERG20 locus of S. cerevisiae WB08, achieving endogenous ERG20 knockout and constructing strain WB09 ( Fig. 4 A). An alternative strategy was also developed: a mitochondrial-targeted ERG20 F96W/N127W and tVvTS M522K/13aa fusion construct was used to knock out endogenous ERG20, generating strain WB10 ( Fig. 4 A). Fermentation results demonstrated that both WB09 and WB10 (with endogenous ERG20 knocked out) exhibited decreased α-terpineol titer and impaired cell growth ( Fig. 4 B). This was likely because reduced intracellular FPP synthesis lowered ergosterol levels (a downstream product of FPP) [ 31 , 32 ]. To mitigate this, we exogenously supplemented 20 mg/L ergosterol into the fermentation medium. While this significantly improved the growth of α-terpineol-producing strains, α-terpineol titer remained notably low ( Fig. 4 C). Insufficient α-terpineol synthase expression emerged as a potential bottleneck. We hypothesized that increasing its gene copy number to boost expression would redirect metabolic flux toward α-terpineol biosynthesis and improve titer.

### 3.4. Enhancing tolerance and mitigating growth-production trade-offs via diploid engineering
α-Terpineol possesses potent antibacterial activity, and its intracellular accumulation can induce significant cytotoxicity even at relatively low titers [ 33 ]. To mitigate α-terpineol toxicity, we selected seven endogenous S. cerevisiae tolerance-associated genes for overexpression screening ( Table S1 ). The candidates were obtained by combining NCBI/database annotations with literature survey. The selection rationale encompassed three protective dimensions: (1) canonical multidrug ABC transporters for extracellular efflux (Pdr5) and vacuolar transporter (Ycf1) of lipophilic xenobiotics [ 34 , 35 ]; (2) mitochondrial membrane transporters and structural components (Atm1, Mic12, Mmr1) to potentially alleviate local toxicity and membrane stress caused by our mitochondrial compartmentalization strategy [ [36] , [37] , [38] ]; and (3) putative stress-responsive clearance proteins (Mga2, Ups1) to evaluate the mitigation of terpene-induced proteotoxic stress [ 39 , 40 ]. These seven candidates were identified and integrated into the HO locus of strain WB02 ( Table S1 ). Among the candidates, overexpression of the ABC transporter Pdr5 yielded the most significant improvement, increasing the α-terpineol titer by 1.22-fold compared to the control ( Fig. 5 A). Notably, compared to the parental strain WB02, all strains overexpressing the tested tolerance-related genes, particularly Pdr5, exhibited improved cell growth. This suggests that even at low production titers, the metabolic burden or inherent cytotoxicity of pathway intermediates can subtly impair cell fitness, and overexpression of tolerance-associated genes overexpression alleviates this stress, thereby promoting better growth. PDR5 is known to enhance β-carotene efflux and improve β-carotene tolerance in S. cerevisiae [ 41 ], and its overexpression may alleviate terpene-associated stress by reducing intracellular toxicity, either through direct export of α-terpineol or through broader detoxification-related effec

### 3.5. Medium optimization and fed-batch fermentation boost α-terpineol titer
Culture medium components affect α-terpineol biosynthesis, and medium optimization is a routine approach to boosting biosynthetic titers [ 42 ]. Key parameters for optimization include adjusting the carbon-to-nitrogen (C/N) ratio and initial pH. Additionally, the α-terpineol synthase used in this study harbors magnesium ion-binding motifs, and the volume fraction of organic extractant also impacts α-terpineol titer. We thus optimized four parameters for WB11 (the highest-titer strain): C/N ratio, Mg 2+ concentration, organic extractant volume fraction, and initial pH. A uniform design using DPS software was used to develop the medium optimization protocol for WB11 ( Table S2 ). The experimental results demonstrated that a C/N ratio of 7:1, pH 6.4, combined with 10 mM Mg 2+ and 25% (v/v) organic phase, yielded the maximum α-terpineol titer of 28.83 ± 2.94 mg/L ( Fig. 6 A). This condition provided an optimal balance between cell growth and terpene synthesis, serving as the basis for the subsequent fed-batch fermentation.

### 4. Discussion
Synthetic biology has enabled the production of various plant-derived monoterpenoids in S. cerevisiae [ 18 , 43 , 44 ]; however, titers for α-terpineol have historically lagged behind those of other terpenes such as limonene and linalool [ 18 , 43 ]. This discrepancy is largely attributed to the complex cyclization mechanism of α-terpineol synthase and the strict regulation of the precursor GPP branch point [ 10 ]. In this study, we established a combinatorial engineering framework addressing three synergistic bottlenecks: catalytic inefficiency, precursor diversion, and cellular toxicity. The resulting strain, WB11, achieved a titer of 81.78 mg/L in a 5-L bioreactor, representing a 1635.6-fold improvement over the initial strain.
In nature, monoterpenoids are predominantly synthesized in plant plastids, and monoterpene synthases typically harbor a plastid-targeting transit peptide at their N-terminus [ 45 ]. Previous studies have demonstrated that truncation of the transit peptide of VvTS is indispensable for its catalytic activity in S. cerevisiae [ 10 ]. Building upon this prior truncation strategy, we further identified redundant sequences within the tVvTS. Subsequent truncation experiments on tVvTS revealed that removing an additional 13 N-terminal amino acids resulted in a two-fold increase in α-terpineol production, representing the best-performing truncation variant under the tested conditions. Notably, truncation of 15 amino acids resulted in an undetectable level of α-terpineol production. We hypothesize that residues 13-15 are located near a structurally important boundary between the flexible N-terminus and the catalytic core. Excessive truncation (i.e., 15 amino acids) is postulated to disrupt the conformational integrity of the catalytic core, thereby abolishing detectable whole-cell production [ 46 ]. This abrupt loss of activity suggests that residues 13–15 may be important for maintaining the structural integrity of the catalytic region. This observ

### Abstract
Plant-derived monoterpenoid α-terpineol has gained significant attention due to its versatile applications in the food, cosmetic and pharmaceutical industries. Microbial biosynthesis offers an environmentally sustainable approach for its commercial-scale production. Here, we developed a combinatorial engineering strategy to enhance α-terpineol production in Saccharomyces cerevisiae . A truncated Vitis vinifera α-terpineol synthase (tVvTS) was optimized through alanine scanning, site-directed mutagenesis, and N-terminal truncation, yielding a variant with improved whole-cell production performance, tVvTS M522K/13aa , which increased α-terpineol titer by 4.8-fold. Further enhancement of mevalonate pathway flux through enzyme fusion and mitochondrial compartmentalization increased the titer by 26.3-fold relative to the parental strain. Subsequent optimization of tolerance-associated genes expression, diploid construction, and fed-batch fermentation enabled the final strain WB11 to produce 81.78 mg/L α-terpineol in a 5-L bioreactor. This study provides an efficient combinatorial strategy for microbial production of natural terpene alcohols.

### 1. Introduction
α-Terpineol is a valuable monoterpenoid widely used in the flavor, fragrance, pharmaceutical, and cosmetic industries because of its pleasant aroma and diverse bioactivities [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. At present, α-terpineol is mainly obtained from plant extraction, which is constrained by seasonal variation, low recovery, and environmental concerns. Chemical synthesis is feasible but often requires toxic solvents and harsh reaction conditions. Therefore, microbial production has emerged as a promising alternative for the sustainable manufacture of α-terpineol and other “natural” terpenoids [ 7 , 8 ].
In microorganisms, α-terpineol is synthesized from geranyl diphosphate (GPP), which is derived from the native isoprenoid pathway [ 9 ]. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae , expression of a truncated α-terpineol synthase from Vitis vinifera (tVvTS), together with pathway engineering of the mevalonate pathway, enabled de novo α-terpineol production, but the reported titers remained low (3.32 mg/L in shake flasks and 21.88 mg/L in a 5-L bioreactor) [ 10 ]. These results indicate that microbial α-terpineol biosynthesis is still far from industrially relevant levels. Three major unresolved bottlenecks appear to limit this process: the low catalytic efficiency and poor heterologous performance of plant-derived VvTS/tVvTS in yeast, severe competition for the common precursor GPP with endogenous sterol biosynthesis, and the cytotoxicity of α-terpineol that impairs cell growth and production [ 11 , 12 ].
Plant-derived terpene synthases often exhibit low catalytic efficiency and poor performance in heterologous hosts [ 13 , 14 ], making enzyme optimization a key strategy for improving monoterpene production. For example, structure-guided protein engineering has been successfully applied to enhance the activities of geraniol synthase and borneol synthase, leading to markedly improved product titers in microbial hosts [ 15 , 16 ]. However, such strategies have not yet been a

### 2.6. α-Terpineol extraction, identification, and quantification
After fermentation of S. cerevisiae strains, 2 mL of the upper organic phase was transferred to a 2 mL Eppendorf (EP) tube and centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 10 min. The clear upper organic phase was carefully aspirated (to avoid impurities) into a clean 2 mL EP tube and recentrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 5 min. The organic phase was extracted using a 1 mL syringe and filtered through a 0.22 μm organic membrane. The clear filtrate was transferred to an HPLC vial insert and analyzed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) on the same day.

### 2.7. Optimization of medium components
In YPD medium, glucose serves as the primary carbon source, whereas yeast extract and peptone serve as the main nitrogen sources. The calculation formula for C/N is as follows:
C / N = C ( g l u c o s e ) N ( y e a s t e x t r a c t + p e p t o n e ) = X 180.156 g · m o l − 1 × 6 ( 10.9 % × Y + 15.4 % × Z ) 14 g · m o l − 1
where X, Y, and Z represent the concentrations (g/L) of glucose, yeast extract, and peptone, respectively. The molecular weight of glucose was taken as 180.156 g/mol, and each glucose molecule contained six carbon atoms. The total nitrogen contents of yeast extract and peptone were assumed to be 10.9% and 15.4%, respectively. The atomic weight of nitrogen was taken as 14 g/mol.

### 3.1. Structure-guided engineering of tVvTS for enhanced α-terpineol production
We introduced tVvTS (N-terminal 28-amino-acid signal peptide removed) [ 10 ] into S . cerevisiae BY4742 to generate strain WB01. Fermentation of WB01 confirmed that tVvTS is functional in α-terpineol biosynthesis ( Fig. S1 ). However, the initial titer was low, reaching only 0.05 mg/L ( Fig. 1 B). To overcome the low apparent in vivo performance of heterologous terpene synthases, a semi-rational design approach was employed. Due to the absence of a crystallographic structure for VvTS, we constructed a high-confidence homology model using SWISS-MODEL. The resulting model exhibited 55.91% sequence identity and a GMQE score of 0.82, suggesting high reliability. We preprocessed the tVvTS protein and GPP as the ligand using AutoDock software, then performed molecular docking with AutoDock Vina and visualized the best docking pose using PyMOL.
Modeling of truncated α-terpineol synthase from Vitis vinifera (tVvTS) and assessment of α-terpineol production in tVvTS mutants. (A) Molecular docking model of tVvTS with GPP, generated with PyMOL, highlighting amino acid residues within 4 Å of the ligand as identified by docking. (B) α-Terpineol production of tVvTS alanine scanning mutants, targeting residues within 4 Å. (C) α-Terpineol production of tVvTS saturation mutants at six identified key positions: K90, Q127, P215, V288, F290, and M522. All data represent the mean ± standard deviation of three biologically independent samples. Key amino acid residues critical for enzyme function are typically located in or near the binding pocket [ 20 , 21 ]. We thus identified potential key residues as those within 4 Å of the tVvTS ligand-binding pocket. From the docking pose, we selected amino acid residues in the substrate binding site, binding pocket entrance, and other related regions for further characterization ( Fig. 1 A). The identified residues were Q81, Y86, K90, Q127, H128, L210, P215, V288, F290, Y294, S448, I451, I520, M522, and M527. We engineered tVvTS by mutating these re

### 3.2. Strengthening precursor supply improves α-terpineol production
HMG-CoA reductase is a rate-limiting enzyme in terpenoid biosynthesis [ 22 ], and expressing its truncated variant (tHMG1) has been shown to improve terpenoid production [ 23 ]. To boost α-terpineol precursor supply, we expressed tHMG1 in yeast to redirect metabolic flux toward terpenoid synthesis ( Fig. 3 A). GPP is the direct precursor of α-terpineol and an intermediate in farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) synthesis catalyzed by Erg20. Erg20 has a higher affinity for GPP than tVvTS M522K/13aa , thereby limiting tVvTS M522K/13aa apparent in vivo performance. To mitigate Erg20-mediated GPP consumption and ensure sufficient precursor for monoterpenoid synthase, we engineered the Erg20 F96W/N127W mutant (with reduced GPP affinity) [ 24 , 25 ]. Spatial proximity of consecutive enzymes in metabolic pathways facilitates substrate channeling and enhances flux efficiency [ 26 , 27 ]. We thus investigated whether fusing ERG20 F96W/N127W with tVvTS M522K/13aa would improve α-terpineol production. The fusion strategy was designed to potentially promote more efficient intermediate transfer between the GPP-generating enzyme (ERG20 F96W/N127W ) and the GPP-consuming α-terpineol synthase, thereby reducing cytoplasmic diffusion and competitive consumption of GPP by endogenous pathways. Prior studies in S. cerevisiae have shown that fusion expression can, in some cases, outperform separate co-expression for monoterpenoid production. We fused ERG20 F96W/N127W to the N-terminus and C-terminus of tVvTS M522K/13aa via linkers (GS) 5 , respectively. These fusion constructs were integrated into the multi-copy rDNA locus of the BY4742 genome to generate strains WB03 and WB04 ( Fig. 3 A). These strategies collectively improved α-terpineol production. Strain WB04 showed a more pronounced increase in α-terpineol titer, reaching 0.84 mg/L. This titer was 3.5-fold higher than that of the parental strain WB02 ( Fig. 3 B). Notably, this 3.5-fold titer improvement is consistent with a possible benefit

### 3.3. Redirecting GPP flux toward α-terpineol biosynthesis
Endogenous Erg20 in yeast converts GPP to FPP, which limits α-terpineol production. To maximize α-terpineol production, we targeted deletion of the endogenous ERG20 gene. We integrated the ERG20 F96W/N127W and tVvT SM522K/13aa fusion protein into the ERG20 locus of S. cerevisiae WB08, achieving endogenous ERG20 knockout and constructing strain WB09 ( Fig. 4 A). An alternative strategy was also developed: a mitochondrial-targeted ERG20 F96W/N127W and tVvTS M522K/13aa fusion construct was used to knock out endogenous ERG20, generating strain WB10 ( Fig. 4 A). Fermentation results demonstrated that both WB09 and WB10 (with endogenous ERG20 knocked out) exhibited decreased α-terpineol titer and impaired cell growth ( Fig. 4 B). This was likely because reduced intracellular FPP synthesis lowered ergosterol levels (a downstream product of FPP) [ 31 , 32 ]. To mitigate this, we exogenously supplemented 20 mg/L ergosterol into the fermentation medium. While this significantly improved the growth of α-terpineol-producing strains, α-terpineol titer remained notably low ( Fig. 4 C). Insufficient α-terpineol synthase expression emerged as a potential bottleneck. We hypothesized that increasing its gene copy number to boost expression would redirect metabolic flux toward α-terpineol biosynthesis and improve titer.

### 3.4. Enhancing tolerance and mitigating growth-production trade-offs via diploid engineering
α-Terpineol possesses potent antibacterial activity, and its intracellular accumulation can induce significant cytotoxicity even at relatively low titers [ 33 ]. To mitigate α-terpineol toxicity, we selected seven endogenous S. cerevisiae tolerance-associated genes for overexpression screening ( Table S1 ). The candidates were obtained by combining NCBI/database annotations with literature survey. The selection rationale encompassed three protective dimensions: (1) canonical multidrug ABC transporters for extracellular efflux (Pdr5) and vacuolar transporter (Ycf1) of lipophilic xenobiotics [ 34 , 35 ]; (2) mitochondrial membrane transporters and structural components (Atm1, Mic12, Mmr1) to potentially alleviate local toxicity and membrane stress caused by our mitochondrial compartmentalization strategy [ [36] , [37] , [38] ]; and (3) putative stress-responsive clearance proteins (Mga2, Ups1) to evaluate the mitigation of terpene-induced proteotoxic stress [ 39 , 40 ]. These seven candidates were identified and integrated into the HO locus of strain WB02 ( Table S1 ). Among the candidates, overexpression of the ABC transporter Pdr5 yielded the most significant improvement, increasing the α-terpineol titer by 1.22-fold compared to the control ( Fig. 5 A). Notably, compared to the parental strain WB02, all strains overexpressing the tested tolerance-related genes, particularly Pdr5, exhibited improved cell growth. This suggests that even at low production titers, the metabolic burden or inherent cytotoxicity of pathway intermediates can subtly impair cell fitness, and overexpression of tolerance-associated genes overexpression alleviates this stress, thereby promoting better growth. PDR5 is known to enhance β-carotene efflux and improve β-carotene tolerance in S. cerevisiae [ 41 ], and its overexpression may alleviate terpene-associated stress by reducing intracellular toxicity, either through direct export of α-terpineol or through broader detoxification-related effec

### 3.5. Medium optimization and fed-batch fermentation boost α-terpineol titer
Culture medium components affect α-terpineol biosynthesis, and medium optimization is a routine approach to boosting biosynthetic titers [ 42 ]. Key parameters for optimization include adjusting the carbon-to-nitrogen (C/N) ratio and initial pH. Additionally, the α-terpineol synthase used in this study harbors magnesium ion-binding motifs, and the volume fraction of organic extractant also impacts α-terpineol titer. We thus optimized four parameters for WB11 (the highest-titer strain): C/N ratio, Mg 2+ concentration, organic extractant volume fraction, and initial pH. A uniform design using DPS software was used to develop the medium optimization protocol for WB11 ( Table S2 ). The experimental results demonstrated that a C/N ratio of 7:1, pH 6.4, combined with 10 mM Mg 2+ and 25% (v/v) organic phase, yielded the maximum α-terpineol titer of 28.83 ± 2.94 mg/L ( Fig. 6 A). This condition provided an optimal balance between cell growth and terpene synthesis, serving as the basis for the subsequent fed-batch fermentation.

### 4. Discussion
Synthetic biology has enabled the production of various plant-derived monoterpenoids in S. cerevisiae [ 18 , 43 , 44 ]; however, titers for α-terpineol have historically lagged behind those of other terpenes such as limonene and linalool [ 18 , 43 ]. This discrepancy is largely attributed to the complex cyclization mechanism of α-terpineol synthase and the strict regulation of the precursor GPP branch point [ 10 ]. In this study, we established a combinatorial engineering framework addressing three synergistic bottlenecks: catalytic inefficiency, precursor diversion, and cellular toxicity. The resulting strain, WB11, achieved a titer of 81.78 mg/L in a 5-L bioreactor, representing a 1635.6-fold improvement over the initial strain.
In nature, monoterpenoids are predominantly synthesized in plant plastids, and monoterpene synthases typically harbor a plastid-targeting transit peptide at their N-terminus [ 45 ]. Previous studies have demonstrated that truncation of the transit peptide of VvTS is indispensable for its catalytic activity in S. cerevisiae [ 10 ]. Building upon this prior truncation strategy, we further identified redundant sequences within the tVvTS. Subsequent truncation experiments on tVvTS revealed that removing an additional 13 N-terminal amino acids resulted in a two-fold increase in α-terpineol production, representing the best-performing truncation variant under the tested conditions. Notably, truncation of 15 amino acids resulted in an undetectable level of α-terpineol production. We hypothesize that residues 13-15 are located near a structurally important boundary between the flexible N-terminus and the catalytic core. Excessive truncation (i.e., 15 amino acids) is postulated to disrupt the conformational integrity of the catalytic core, thereby abolishing detectable whole-cell production [ 46 ]. This abrupt loss of activity suggests that residues 13–15 may be important for maintaining the structural integrity of the catalytic region. This observ

### Abstract
Plant-derived monoterpenoid α-terpineol has gained significant attention due to its versatile applications in the food, cosmetic and pharmaceutical industries. Microbial biosynthesis offers an environmentally sustainable approach for its commercial-scale production. Here, we developed a combinatorial engineering strategy to enhance α-terpineol production in Saccharomyces cerevisiae . A truncated Vitis vinifera α-terpineol synthase (tVvTS) was optimized through alanine scanning, site-directed mutagenesis, and N-terminal truncation, yielding a variant with improved whole-cell production performance, tVvTS M522K/13aa , which increased α-terpineol titer by 4.8-fold. Further enhancement of mevalonate pathway flux through enzyme fusion and mitochondrial compartmentalization increased the titer by 26.3-fold relative to the parental strain. Subsequent optimization of tolerance-associated genes expression, diploid construction, and fed-batch fermentation enabled the final strain WB11 to produce 81.78 mg/L α-terpineol in a 5-L bioreactor. This study provides an efficient combinatorial strategy for microbial production of natural terpene alcohols.

### 1. Introduction
α-Terpineol is a valuable monoterpenoid widely used in the flavor, fragrance, pharmaceutical, and cosmetic industries because of its pleasant aroma and diverse bioactivities [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. At present, α-terpineol is mainly obtained from plant extraction, which is constrained by seasonal variation, low recovery, and environmental concerns. Chemical synthesis is feasible but often requires toxic solvents and harsh reaction conditions. Therefore, microbial production has emerged as a promising alternative for the sustainable manufacture of α-terpineol and other “natural” terpenoids [ 7 , 8 ].
In microorganisms, α-terpineol is synthesized from geranyl diphosphate (GPP), which is derived from the native isoprenoid pathway [ 9 ]. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae , expression of a truncated α-terpineol synthase from Vitis vinifera (tVvTS), together with pathway engineering of the mevalonate pathway, enabled de novo α-terpineol production, but the reported titers remained low (3.32 mg/L in shake flasks and 21.88 mg/L in a 5-L bioreactor) [ 10 ]. These results indicate that microbial α-terpineol biosynthesis is still far from industrially relevant levels. Three major unresolved bottlenecks appear to limit this process: the low catalytic efficiency and poor heterologous performance of plant-derived VvTS/tVvTS in yeast, severe competition for the common precursor GPP with endogenous sterol biosynthesis, and the cytotoxicity of α-terpineol that impairs cell growth and production [ 11 , 12 ].
Plant-derived terpene synthases often exhibit low catalytic efficiency and poor performance in heterologous hosts [ 13 , 14 ], making enzyme optimization a key strategy for improving monoterpene production. For example, structure-guided protein engineering has been successfully applied to enhance the activities of geraniol synthase and borneol synthase, leading to markedly improved product titers in microbial hosts [ 15 , 16 ]. However, such strategies have not yet been a

### 2.6. α-Terpineol extraction, identification, and quantification
After fermentation of S. cerevisiae strains, 2 mL of the upper organic phase was transferred to a 2 mL Eppendorf (EP) tube and centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 10 min. The clear upper organic phase was carefully aspirated (to avoid impurities) into a clean 2 mL EP tube and recentrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 5 min. The organic phase was extracted using a 1 mL syringe and filtered through a 0.22 μm organic membrane. The clear filtrate was transferred to an HPLC vial insert and analyzed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) on the same day.

### 2.7. Optimization of medium components
In YPD medium, glucose serves as the primary carbon source, whereas yeast extract and peptone serve as the main nitrogen sources. The calculation formula for C/N is as follows:
C / N = C ( g l u c o s e ) N ( y e a s t e x t r a c t + p e p t o n e ) = X 180.156 g · m o l − 1 × 6 ( 10.9 % × Y + 15.4 % × Z ) 14 g · m o l − 1
where X, Y, and Z represent the concentrations (g/L) of glucose, yeast extract, and peptone, respectively. The molecular weight of glucose was taken as 180.156 g/mol, and each glucose molecule contained six carbon atoms. The total nitrogen contents of yeast extract and peptone were assumed to be 10.9% and 15.4%, respectively. The atomic weight of nitrogen was taken as 14 g/mol.

### 3.1. Structure-guided engineering of tVvTS for enhanced α-terpineol production
We introduced tVvTS (N-terminal 28-amino-acid signal peptide removed) [ 10 ] into S . cerevisiae BY4742 to generate strain WB01. Fermentation of WB01 confirmed that tVvTS is functional in α-terpineol biosynthesis ( Fig. S1 ). However, the initial titer was low, reaching only 0.05 mg/L ( Fig. 1 B). To overcome the low apparent in vivo performance of heterologous terpene synthases, a semi-rational design approach was employed. Due to the absence of a crystallographic structure for VvTS, we constructed a high-confidence homology model using SWISS-MODEL. The resulting model exhibited 55.91% sequence identity and a GMQE score of 0.82, suggesting high reliability. We preprocessed the tVvTS protein and GPP as the ligand using AutoDock software, then performed molecular docking with AutoDock Vina and visualized the best docking pose using PyMOL.
Modeling of truncated α-terpineol synthase from Vitis vinifera (tVvTS) and assessment of α-terpineol production in tVvTS mutants. (A) Molecular docking model of tVvTS with GPP, generated with PyMOL, highlighting amino acid residues within 4 Å of the ligand as identified by docking. (B) α-Terpineol production of tVvTS alanine scanning mutants, targeting residues within 4 Å. (C) α-Terpineol production of tVvTS saturation mutants at six identified key positions: K90, Q127, P215, V288, F290, and M522. All data represent the mean ± standard deviation of three biologically independent samples. Key amino acid residues critical for enzyme function are typically located in or near the binding pocket [ 20 , 21 ]. We thus identified potential key residues as those within 4 Å of the tVvTS ligand-binding pocket. From the docking pose, we selected amino acid residues in the substrate binding site, binding pocket entrance, and other related regions for further characterization ( Fig. 1 A). The identified residues were Q81, Y86, K90, Q127, H128, L210, P215, V288, F290, Y294, S448, I451, I520, M522, and M527. We engineered tVvTS by mutating these re

### 3.2. Strengthening precursor supply improves α-terpineol production
HMG-CoA reductase is a rate-limiting enzyme in terpenoid biosynthesis [ 22 ], and expressing its truncated variant (tHMG1) has been shown to improve terpenoid production [ 23 ]. To boost α-terpineol precursor supply, we expressed tHMG1 in yeast to redirect metabolic flux toward terpenoid synthesis ( Fig. 3 A). GPP is the direct precursor of α-terpineol and an intermediate in farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) synthesis catalyzed by Erg20. Erg20 has a higher affinity for GPP than tVvTS M522K/13aa , thereby limiting tVvTS M522K/13aa apparent in vivo performance. To mitigate Erg20-mediated GPP consumption and ensure sufficient precursor for monoterpenoid synthase, we engineered the Erg20 F96W/N127W mutant (with reduced GPP affinity) [ 24 , 25 ]. Spatial proximity of consecutive enzymes in metabolic pathways facilitates substrate channeling and enhances flux efficiency [ 26 , 27 ]. We thus investigated whether fusing ERG20 F96W/N127W with tVvTS M522K/13aa would improve α-terpineol production. The fusion strategy was designed to potentially promote more efficient intermediate transfer between the GPP-generating enzyme (ERG20 F96W/N127W ) and the GPP-consuming α-terpineol synthase, thereby reducing cytoplasmic diffusion and competitive consumption of GPP by endogenous pathways. Prior studies in S. cerevisiae have shown that fusion expression can, in some cases, outperform separate co-expression for monoterpenoid production. We fused ERG20 F96W/N127W to the N-terminus and C-terminus of tVvTS M522K/13aa via linkers (GS) 5 , respectively. These fusion constructs were integrated into the multi-copy rDNA locus of the BY4742 genome to generate strains WB03 and WB04 ( Fig. 3 A). These strategies collectively improved α-terpineol production. Strain WB04 showed a more pronounced increase in α-terpineol titer, reaching 0.84 mg/L. This titer was 3.5-fold higher than that of the parental strain WB02 ( Fig. 3 B). Notably, this 3.5-fold titer improvement is consistent with a possible benefit

### 3.3. Redirecting GPP flux toward α-terpineol biosynthesis
Endogenous Erg20 in yeast converts GPP to FPP, which limits α-terpineol production. To maximize α-terpineol production, we targeted deletion of the endogenous ERG20 gene. We integrated the ERG20 F96W/N127W and tVvT SM522K/13aa fusion protein into the ERG20 locus of S. cerevisiae WB08, achieving endogenous ERG20 knockout and constructing strain WB09 ( Fig. 4 A). An alternative strategy was also developed: a mitochondrial-targeted ERG20 F96W/N127W and tVvTS M522K/13aa fusion construct was used to knock out endogenous ERG20, generating strain WB10 ( Fig. 4 A). Fermentation results demonstrated that both WB09 and WB10 (with endogenous ERG20 knocked out) exhibited decreased α-terpineol titer and impaired cell growth ( Fig. 4 B). This was likely because reduced intracellular FPP synthesis lowered ergosterol levels (a downstream product of FPP) [ 31 , 32 ]. To mitigate this, we exogenously supplemented 20 mg/L ergosterol into the fermentation medium. While this significantly improved the growth of α-terpineol-producing strains, α-terpineol titer remained notably low ( Fig. 4 C). Insufficient α-terpineol synthase expression emerged as a potential bottleneck. We hypothesized that increasing its gene copy number to boost expression would redirect metabolic flux toward α-terpineol biosynthesis and improve titer.

### 3.4. Enhancing tolerance and mitigating growth-production trade-offs via diploid engineering
α-Terpineol possesses potent antibacterial activity, and its intracellular accumulation can induce significant cytotoxicity even at relatively low titers [ 33 ]. To mitigate α-terpineol toxicity, we selected seven endogenous S. cerevisiae tolerance-associated genes for overexpression screening ( Table S1 ). The candidates were obtained by combining NCBI/database annotations with literature survey. The selection rationale encompassed three protective dimensions: (1) canonical multidrug ABC transporters for extracellular efflux (Pdr5) and vacuolar transporter (Ycf1) of lipophilic xenobiotics [ 34 , 35 ]; (2) mitochondrial membrane transporters and structural components (Atm1, Mic12, Mmr1) to potentially alleviate local toxicity and membrane stress caused by our mitochondrial compartmentalization strategy [ [36] , [37] , [38] ]; and (3) putative stress-responsive clearance proteins (Mga2, Ups1) to evaluate the mitigation of terpene-induced proteotoxic stress [ 39 , 40 ]. These seven candidates were identified and integrated into the HO locus of strain WB02 ( Table S1 ). Among the candidates, overexpression of the ABC transporter Pdr5 yielded the most significant improvement, increasing the α-terpineol titer by 1.22-fold compared to the control ( Fig. 5 A). Notably, compared to the parental strain WB02, all strains overexpressing the tested tolerance-related genes, particularly Pdr5, exhibited improved cell growth. This suggests that even at low production titers, the metabolic burden or inherent cytotoxicity of pathway intermediates can subtly impair cell fitness, and overexpression of tolerance-associated genes overexpression alleviates this stress, thereby promoting better growth. PDR5 is known to enhance β-carotene efflux and improve β-carotene tolerance in S. cerevisiae [ 41 ], and its overexpression may alleviate terpene-associated stress by reducing intracellular toxicity, either through direct export of α-terpineol or through broader detoxification-related effec

### 3.5. Medium optimization and fed-batch fermentation boost α-terpineol titer
Culture medium components affect α-terpineol biosynthesis, and medium optimization is a routine approach to boosting biosynthetic titers [ 42 ]. Key parameters for optimization include adjusting the carbon-to-nitrogen (C/N) ratio and initial pH. Additionally, the α-terpineol synthase used in this study harbors magnesium ion-binding motifs, and the volume fraction of organic extractant also impacts α-terpineol titer. We thus optimized four parameters for WB11 (the highest-titer strain): C/N ratio, Mg 2+ concentration, organic extractant volume fraction, and initial pH. A uniform design using DPS software was used to develop the medium optimization protocol for WB11 ( Table S2 ). The experimental results demonstrated that a C/N ratio of 7:1, pH 6.4, combined with 10 mM Mg 2+ and 25% (v/v) organic phase, yielded the maximum α-terpineol titer of 28.83 ± 2.94 mg/L ( Fig. 6 A). This condition provided an optimal balance between cell growth and terpene synthesis, serving as the basis for the subsequent fed-batch fermentation.

### 4. Discussion
Synthetic biology has enabled the production of various plant-derived monoterpenoids in S. cerevisiae [ 18 , 43 , 44 ]; however, titers for α-terpineol have historically lagged behind those of other terpenes such as limonene and linalool [ 18 , 43 ]. This discrepancy is largely attributed to the complex cyclization mechanism of α-terpineol synthase and the strict regulation of the precursor GPP branch point [ 10 ]. In this study, we established a combinatorial engineering framework addressing three synergistic bottlenecks: catalytic inefficiency, precursor diversion, and cellular toxicity. The resulting strain, WB11, achieved a titer of 81.78 mg/L in a 5-L bioreactor, representing a 1635.6-fold improvement over the initial strain.
In nature, monoterpenoids are predominantly synthesized in plant plastids, and monoterpene synthases typically harbor a plastid-targeting transit peptide at their N-terminus [ 45 ]. Previous studies have demonstrated that truncation of the transit peptide of VvTS is indispensable for its catalytic activity in S. cerevisiae [ 10 ]. Building upon this prior truncation strategy, we further identified redundant sequences within the tVvTS. Subsequent truncation experiments on tVvTS revealed that removing an additional 13 N-terminal amino acids resulted in a two-fold increase in α-terpineol production, representing the best-performing truncation variant under the tested conditions. Notably, truncation of 15 amino acids resulted in an undetectable level of α-terpineol production. We hypothesize that residues 13-15 are located near a structurally important boundary between the flexible N-terminus and the catalytic core. Excessive truncation (i.e., 15 amino acids) is postulated to disrupt the conformational integrity of the catalytic core, thereby abolishing detectable whole-cell production [ 46 ]. This abrupt loss of activity suggests that residues 13–15 may be important for maintaining the structural integrity of the catalytic region. This observ

### Abstract
Plant-derived monoterpenoid α-terpineol has gained significant attention due to its versatile applications in the food, cosmetic and pharmaceutical industries. Microbial biosynthesis offers an environmentally sustainable approach for its commercial-scale production. Here, we developed a combinatorial engineering strategy to enhance α-terpineol production in Saccharomyces cerevisiae . A truncated Vitis vinifera α-terpineol synthase (tVvTS) was optimized through alanine scanning, site-directed mutagenesis, and N-terminal truncation, yielding a variant with improved whole-cell production performance, tVvTS M522K/13aa , which increased α-terpineol titer by 4.8-fold. Further enhancement of mevalonate pathway flux through enzyme fusion and mitochondrial compartmentalization increased the titer by 26.3-fold relative to the parental strain. Subsequent optimization of tolerance-associated genes expression, diploid construction, and fed-batch fermentation enabled the final strain WB11 to produce 81.78 mg/L α-terpineol in a 5-L bioreactor. This study provides an efficient combinatorial strategy for microbial production of natural terpene alcohols.

### 1. Introduction
α-Terpineol is a valuable monoterpenoid widely used in the flavor, fragrance, pharmaceutical, and cosmetic industries because of its pleasant aroma and diverse bioactivities [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. At present, α-terpineol is mainly obtained from plant extraction, which is constrained by seasonal variation, low recovery, and environmental concerns. Chemical synthesis is feasible but often requires toxic solvents and harsh reaction conditions. Therefore, microbial production has emerged as a promising alternative for the sustainable manufacture of α-terpineol and other “natural” terpenoids [ 7 , 8 ].
In microorganisms, α-terpineol is synthesized from geranyl diphosphate (GPP), which is derived from the native isoprenoid pathway [ 9 ]. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae , expression of a truncated α-terpineol synthase from Vitis vinifera (tVvTS), together with pathway engineering of the mevalonate pathway, enabled de novo α-terpineol production, but the reported titers remained low (3.32 mg/L in shake flasks and 21.88 mg/L in a 5-L bioreactor) [ 10 ]. These results indicate that microbial α-terpineol biosynthesis is still far from industrially relevant levels. Three major unresolved bottlenecks appear to limit this process: the low catalytic efficiency and poor heterologous performance of plant-derived VvTS/tVvTS in yeast, severe competition for the common precursor GPP with endogenous sterol biosynthesis, and the cytotoxicity of α-terpineol that impairs cell growth and production [ 11 , 12 ].
Plant-derived terpene synthases often exhibit low catalytic efficiency and poor performance in heterologous hosts [ 13 , 14 ], making enzyme optimization a key strategy for improving monoterpene production. For example, structure-guided protein engineering has been successfully applied to enhance the activities of geraniol synthase and borneol synthase, leading to markedly improved product titers in microbial hosts [ 15 , 16 ]. However, such strategies have not yet been a

### 2.6. α-Terpineol extraction, identification, and quantification
After fermentation of S. cerevisiae strains, 2 mL of the upper organic phase was transferred to a 2 mL Eppendorf (EP) tube and centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 10 min. The clear upper organic phase was carefully aspirated (to avoid impurities) into a clean 2 mL EP tube and recentrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 5 min. The organic phase was extracted using a 1 mL syringe and filtered through a 0.22 μm organic membrane. The clear filtrate was transferred to an HPLC vial insert and analyzed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) on the same day.

### 2.7. Optimization of medium components
In YPD medium, glucose serves as the primary carbon source, whereas yeast extract and peptone serve as the main nitrogen sources. The calculation formula for C/N is as follows:
C / N = C ( g l u c o s e ) N ( y e a s t e x t r a c t + p e p t o n e ) = X 180.156 g · m o l − 1 × 6 ( 10.9 % × Y + 15.4 % × Z ) 14 g · m o l − 1
where X, Y, and Z represent the concentrations (g/L) of glucose, yeast extract, and peptone, respectively. The molecular weight of glucose was taken as 180.156 g/mol, and each glucose molecule contained six carbon atoms. The total nitrogen contents of yeast extract and peptone were assumed to be 10.9% and 15.4%, respectively. The atomic weight of nitrogen was taken as 14 g/mol.

### 3.1. Structure-guided engineering of tVvTS for enhanced α-terpineol production
We introduced tVvTS (N-terminal 28-amino-acid signal peptide removed) [ 10 ] into S . cerevisiae BY4742 to generate strain WB01. Fermentation of WB01 confirmed that tVvTS is functional in α-terpineol biosynthesis ( Fig. S1 ). However, the initial titer was low, reaching only 0.05 mg/L ( Fig. 1 B). To overcome the low apparent in vivo performance of heterologous terpene synthases, a semi-rational design approach was employed. Due to the absence of a crystallographic structure for VvTS, we constructed a high-confidence homology model using SWISS-MODEL. The resulting model exhibited 55.91% sequence identity and a GMQE score of 0.82, suggesting high reliability. We preprocessed the tVvTS protein and GPP as the ligand using AutoDock software, then performed molecular docking with AutoDock Vina and visualized the best docking pose using PyMOL.
Modeling of truncated α-terpineol synthase from Vitis vinifera (tVvTS) and assessment of α-terpineol production in tVvTS mutants. (A) Molecular docking model of tVvTS with GPP, generated with PyMOL, highlighting amino acid residues within 4 Å of the ligand as identified by docking. (B) α-Terpineol production of tVvTS alanine scanning mutants, targeting residues within 4 Å. (C) α-Terpineol production of tVvTS saturation mutants at six identified key positions: K90, Q127, P215, V288, F290, and M522. All data represent the mean ± standard deviation of three biologically independent samples. Key amino acid residues critical for enzyme function are typically located in or near the binding pocket [ 20 , 21 ]. We thus identified potential key residues as those within 4 Å of the tVvTS ligand-binding pocket. From the docking pose, we selected amino acid residues in the substrate binding site, binding pocket entrance, and other related regions for further characterization ( Fig. 1 A). The identified residues were Q81, Y86, K90, Q127, H128, L210, P215, V288, F290, Y294, S448, I451, I520, M522, and M527. We engineered tVvTS by mutating these re

### 3.2. Strengthening precursor supply improves α-terpineol production
HMG-CoA reductase is a rate-limiting enzyme in terpenoid biosynthesis [ 22 ], and expressing its truncated variant (tHMG1) has been shown to improve terpenoid production [ 23 ]. To boost α-terpineol precursor supply, we expressed tHMG1 in yeast to redirect metabolic flux toward terpenoid synthesis ( Fig. 3 A). GPP is the direct precursor of α-terpineol and an intermediate in farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) synthesis catalyzed by Erg20. Erg20 has a higher affinity for GPP than tVvTS M522K/13aa , thereby limiting tVvTS M522K/13aa apparent in vivo performance. To mitigate Erg20-mediated GPP consumption and ensure sufficient precursor for monoterpenoid synthase, we engineered the Erg20 F96W/N127W mutant (with reduced GPP affinity) [ 24 , 25 ]. Spatial proximity of consecutive enzymes in metabolic pathways facilitates substrate channeling and enhances flux efficiency [ 26 , 27 ]. We thus investigated whether fusing ERG20 F96W/N127W with tVvTS M522K/13aa would improve α-terpineol production. The fusion strategy was designed to potentially promote more efficient intermediate transfer between the GPP-generating enzyme (ERG20 F96W/N127W ) and the GPP-consuming α-terpineol synthase, thereby reducing cytoplasmic diffusion and competitive consumption of GPP by endogenous pathways. Prior studies in S. cerevisiae have shown that fusion expression can, in some cases, outperform separate co-expression for monoterpenoid production. We fused ERG20 F96W/N127W to the N-terminus and C-terminus of tVvTS M522K/13aa via linkers (GS) 5 , respectively. These fusion constructs were integrated into the multi-copy rDNA locus of the BY4742 genome to generate strains WB03 and WB04 ( Fig. 3 A). These strategies collectively improved α-terpineol production. Strain WB04 showed a more pronounced increase in α-terpineol titer, reaching 0.84 mg/L. This titer was 3.5-fold higher than that of the parental strain WB02 ( Fig. 3 B). Notably, this 3.5-fold titer improvement is consistent with a possible benefit

### 3.3. Redirecting GPP flux toward α-terpineol biosynthesis
Endogenous Erg20 in yeast converts GPP to FPP, which limits α-terpineol production. To maximize α-terpineol production, we targeted deletion of the endogenous ERG20 gene. We integrated the ERG20 F96W/N127W and tVvT SM522K/13aa fusion protein into the ERG20 locus of S. cerevisiae WB08, achieving endogenous ERG20 knockout and constructing strain WB09 ( Fig. 4 A). An alternative strategy was also developed: a mitochondrial-targeted ERG20 F96W/N127W and tVvTS M522K/13aa fusion construct was used to knock out endogenous ERG20, generating strain WB10 ( Fig. 4 A). Fermentation results demonstrated that both WB09 and WB10 (with endogenous ERG20 knocked out) exhibited decreased α-terpineol titer and impaired cell growth ( Fig. 4 B). This was likely because reduced intracellular FPP synthesis lowered ergosterol levels (a downstream product of FPP) [ 31 , 32 ]. To mitigate this, we exogenously supplemented 20 mg/L ergosterol into the fermentation medium. While this significantly improved the growth of α-terpineol-producing strains, α-terpineol titer remained notably low ( Fig. 4 C). Insufficient α-terpineol synthase expression emerged as a potential bottleneck. We hypothesized that increasing its gene copy number to boost expression would redirect metabolic flux toward α-terpineol biosynthesis and improve titer.

### 3.4. Enhancing tolerance and mitigating growth-production trade-offs via diploid engineering
α-Terpineol possesses potent antibacterial activity, and its intracellular accumulation can induce significant cytotoxicity even at relatively low titers [ 33 ]. To mitigate α-terpineol toxicity, we selected seven endogenous S. cerevisiae tolerance-associated genes for overexpression screening ( Table S1 ). The candidates were obtained by combining NCBI/database annotations with literature survey. The selection rationale encompassed three protective dimensions: (1) canonical multidrug ABC transporters for extracellular efflux (Pdr5) and vacuolar transporter (Ycf1) of lipophilic xenobiotics [ 34 , 35 ]; (2) mitochondrial membrane transporters and structural components (Atm1, Mic12, Mmr1) to potentially alleviate local toxicity and membrane stress caused by our mitochondrial compartmentalization strategy [ [36] , [37] , [38] ]; and (3) putative stress-responsive clearance proteins (Mga2, Ups1) to evaluate the mitigation of terpene-induced proteotoxic stress [ 39 , 40 ]. These seven candidates were identified and integrated into the HO locus of strain WB02 ( Table S1 ). Among the candidates, overexpression of the ABC transporter Pdr5 yielded the most significant improvement, increasing the α-terpineol titer by 1.22-fold compared to the control ( Fig. 5 A). Notably, compared to the parental strain WB02, all strains overexpressing the tested tolerance-related genes, particularly Pdr5, exhibited improved cell growth. This suggests that even at low production titers, the metabolic burden or inherent cytotoxicity of pathway intermediates can subtly impair cell fitness, and overexpression of tolerance-associated genes overexpression alleviates this stress, thereby promoting better growth. PDR5 is known to enhance β-carotene efflux and improve β-carotene tolerance in S. cerevisiae [ 41 ], and its overexpression may alleviate terpene-associated stress by reducing intracellular toxicity, either through direct export of α-terpineol or through broader detoxification-related effec

### 3.5. Medium optimization and fed-batch fermentation boost α-terpineol titer
Culture medium components affect α-terpineol biosynthesis, and medium optimization is a routine approach to boosting biosynthetic titers [ 42 ]. Key parameters for optimization include adjusting the carbon-to-nitrogen (C/N) ratio and initial pH. Additionally, the α-terpineol synthase used in this study harbors magnesium ion-binding motifs, and the volume fraction of organic extractant also impacts α-terpineol titer. We thus optimized four parameters for WB11 (the highest-titer strain): C/N ratio, Mg 2+ concentration, organic extractant volume fraction, and initial pH. A uniform design using DPS software was used to develop the medium optimization protocol for WB11 ( Table S2 ). The experimental results demonstrated that a C/N ratio of 7:1, pH 6.4, combined with 10 mM Mg 2+ and 25% (v/v) organic phase, yielded the maximum α-terpineol titer of 28.83 ± 2.94 mg/L ( Fig. 6 A). This condition provided an optimal balance between cell growth and terpene synthesis, serving as the basis for the subsequent fed-batch fermentation.

### 4. Discussion
Synthetic biology has enabled the production of various plant-derived monoterpenoids in S. cerevisiae [ 18 , 43 , 44 ]; however, titers for α-terpineol have historically lagged behind those of other terpenes such as limonene and linalool [ 18 , 43 ]. This discrepancy is largely attributed to the complex cyclization mechanism of α-terpineol synthase and the strict regulation of the precursor GPP branch point [ 10 ]. In this study, we established a combinatorial engineering framework addressing three synergistic bottlenecks: catalytic inefficiency, precursor diversion, and cellular toxicity. The resulting strain, WB11, achieved a titer of 81.78 mg/L in a 5-L bioreactor, representing a 1635.6-fold improvement over the initial strain.
In nature, monoterpenoids are predominantly synthesized in plant plastids, and monoterpene synthases typically harbor a plastid-targeting transit peptide at their N-terminus [ 45 ]. Previous studies have demonstrated that truncation of the transit peptide of VvTS is indispensable for its catalytic activity in S. cerevisiae [ 10 ]. Building upon this prior truncation strategy, we further identified redundant sequences within the tVvTS. Subsequent truncation experiments on tVvTS revealed that removing an additional 13 N-terminal amino acids resulted in a two-fold increase in α-terpineol production, representing the best-performing truncation variant under the tested conditions. Notably, truncation of 15 amino acids resulted in an undetectable level of α-terpineol production. We hypothesize that residues 13-15 are located near a structurally important boundary between the flexible N-terminus and the catalytic core. Excessive truncation (i.e., 15 amino acids) is postulated to disrupt the conformational integrity of the catalytic core, thereby abolishing detectable whole-cell production [ 46 ]. This abrupt loss of activity suggests that residues 13–15 may be important for maintaining the structural integrity of the catalytic region. This observ

### Abstract
Plant-derived monoterpenoid α-terpineol has gained significant attention due to its versatile applications in the food, cosmetic and pharmaceutical industries. Microbial biosynthesis offers an environmentally sustainable approach for its commercial-scale production. Here, we developed a combinatorial engineering strategy to enhance α-terpineol production in Saccharomyces cerevisiae . A truncated Vitis vinifera α-terpineol synthase (tVvTS) was optimized through alanine scanning, site-directed mutagenesis, and N-terminal truncation, yielding a variant with improved whole-cell production performance, tVvTS M522K/13aa , which increased α-terpineol titer by 4.8-fold. Further enhancement of mevalonate pathway flux through enzyme fusion and mitochondrial compartmentalization increased the titer by 26.3-fold relative to the parental strain. Subsequent optimization of tolerance-associated genes expression, diploid construction, and fed-batch fermentation enabled the final strain WB11 to produce 81.78 mg/L α-terpineol in a 5-L bioreactor. This study provides an efficient combinatorial strategy for microbial production of natural terpene alcohols.

### 1. Introduction
α-Terpineol is a valuable monoterpenoid widely used in the flavor, fragrance, pharmaceutical, and cosmetic industries because of its pleasant aroma and diverse bioactivities [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. At present, α-terpineol is mainly obtained from plant extraction, which is constrained by seasonal variation, low recovery, and environmental concerns. Chemical synthesis is feasible but often requires toxic solvents and harsh reaction conditions. Therefore, microbial production has emerged as a promising alternative for the sustainable manufacture of α-terpineol and other “natural” terpenoids [ 7 , 8 ].
In microorganisms, α-terpineol is synthesized from geranyl diphosphate (GPP), which is derived from the native isoprenoid pathway [ 9 ]. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae , expression of a truncated α-terpineol synthase from Vitis vinifera (tVvTS), together with pathway engineering of the mevalonate pathway, enabled de novo α-terpineol production, but the reported titers remained low (3.32 mg/L in shake flasks and 21.88 mg/L in a 5-L bioreactor) [ 10 ]. These results indicate that microbial α-terpineol biosynthesis is still far from industrially relevant levels. Three major unresolved bottlenecks appear to limit this process: the low catalytic efficiency and poor heterologous performance of plant-derived VvTS/tVvTS in yeast, severe competition for the common precursor GPP with endogenous sterol biosynthesis, and the cytotoxicity of α-terpineol that impairs cell growth and production [ 11 , 12 ].
Plant-derived terpene synthases often exhibit low catalytic efficiency and poor performance in heterologous hosts [ 13 , 14 ], making enzyme optimization a key strategy for improving monoterpene production. For example, structure-guided protein engineering has been successfully applied to enhance the activities of geraniol synthase and borneol synthase, leading to markedly improved product titers in microbial hosts [ 15 , 16 ]. However, such strategies have not yet been a

### 2.6. α-Terpineol extraction, identification, and quantification
After fermentation of S. cerevisiae strains, 2 mL of the upper organic phase was transferred to a 2 mL Eppendorf (EP) tube and centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 10 min. The clear upper organic phase was carefully aspirated (to avoid impurities) into a clean 2 mL EP tube and recentrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 5 min. The organic phase was extracted using a 1 mL syringe and filtered through a 0.22 μm organic membrane. The clear filtrate was transferred to an HPLC vial insert and analyzed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) on the same day.

### 2.7. Optimization of medium components
In YPD medium, glucose serves as the primary carbon source, whereas yeast extract and peptone serve as the main nitrogen sources. The calculation formula for C/N is as follows:
C / N = C ( g l u c o s e ) N ( y e a s t e x t r a c t + p e p t o n e ) = X 180.156 g · m o l − 1 × 6 ( 10.9 % × Y + 15.4 % × Z ) 14 g · m o l − 1
where X, Y, and Z represent the concentrations (g/L) of glucose, yeast extract, and peptone, respectively. The molecular weight of glucose was taken as 180.156 g/mol, and each glucose molecule contained six carbon atoms. The total nitrogen contents of yeast extract and peptone were assumed to be 10.9% and 15.4%, respectively. The atomic weight of nitrogen was taken as 14 g/mol.

### 3.1. Structure-guided engineering of tVvTS for enhanced α-terpineol production
We introduced tVvTS (N-terminal 28-amino-acid signal peptide removed) [ 10 ] into S . cerevisiae BY4742 to generate strain WB01. Fermentation of WB01 confirmed that tVvTS is functional in α-terpineol biosynthesis ( Fig. S1 ). However, the initial titer was low, reaching only 0.05 mg/L ( Fig. 1 B). To overcome the low apparent in vivo performance of heterologous terpene synthases, a semi-rational design approach was employed. Due to the absence of a crystallographic structure for VvTS, we constructed a high-confidence homology model using SWISS-MODEL. The resulting model exhibited 55.91% sequence identity and a GMQE score of 0.82, suggesting high reliability. We preprocessed the tVvTS protein and GPP as the ligand using AutoDock software, then performed molecular docking with AutoDock Vina and visualized the best docking pose using PyMOL.
Modeling of truncated α-terpineol synthase from Vitis vinifera (tVvTS) and assessment of α-terpineol production in tVvTS mutants. (A) Molecular docking model of tVvTS with GPP, generated with PyMOL, highlighting amino acid residues within 4 Å of the ligand as identified by docking. (B) α-Terpineol production of tVvTS alanine scanning mutants, targeting residues within 4 Å. (C) α-Terpineol production of tVvTS saturation mutants at six identified key positions: K90, Q127, P215, V288, F290, and M522. All data represent the mean ± standard deviation of three biologically independent samples. Key amino acid residues critical for enzyme function are typically located in or near the binding pocket [ 20 , 21 ]. We thus identified potential key residues as those within 4 Å of the tVvTS ligand-binding pocket. From the docking pose, we selected amino acid residues in the substrate binding site, binding pocket entrance, and other related regions for further characterization ( Fig. 1 A). The identified residues were Q81, Y86, K90, Q127, H128, L210, P215, V288, F290, Y294, S448, I451, I520, M522, and M527. We engineered tVvTS by mutating these re

### 3.2. Strengthening precursor supply improves α-terpineol production
HMG-CoA reductase is a rate-limiting enzyme in terpenoid biosynthesis [ 22 ], and expressing its truncated variant (tHMG1) has been shown to improve terpenoid production [ 23 ]. To boost α-terpineol precursor supply, we expressed tHMG1 in yeast to redirect metabolic flux toward terpenoid synthesis ( Fig. 3 A). GPP is the direct precursor of α-terpineol and an intermediate in farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) synthesis catalyzed by Erg20. Erg20 has a higher affinity for GPP than tVvTS M522K/13aa , thereby limiting tVvTS M522K/13aa apparent in vivo performance. To mitigate Erg20-mediated GPP consumption and ensure sufficient precursor for monoterpenoid synthase, we engineered the Erg20 F96W/N127W mutant (with reduced GPP affinity) [ 24 , 25 ]. Spatial proximity of consecutive enzymes in metabolic pathways facilitates substrate channeling and enhances flux efficiency [ 26 , 27 ]. We thus investigated whether fusing ERG20 F96W/N127W with tVvTS M522K/13aa would improve α-terpineol production. The fusion strategy was designed to potentially promote more efficient intermediate transfer between the GPP-generating enzyme (ERG20 F96W/N127W ) and the GPP-consuming α-terpineol synthase, thereby reducing cytoplasmic diffusion and competitive consumption of GPP by endogenous pathways. Prior studies in S. cerevisiae have shown that fusion expression can, in some cases, outperform separate co-expression for monoterpenoid production. We fused ERG20 F96W/N127W to the N-terminus and C-terminus of tVvTS M522K/13aa via linkers (GS) 5 , respectively. These fusion constructs were integrated into the multi-copy rDNA locus of the BY4742 genome to generate strains WB03 and WB04 ( Fig. 3 A). These strategies collectively improved α-terpineol production. Strain WB04 showed a more pronounced increase in α-terpineol titer, reaching 0.84 mg/L. This titer was 3.5-fold higher than that of the parental strain WB02 ( Fig. 3 B). Notably, this 3.5-fold titer improvement is consistent with a possible benefit

### 3.3. Redirecting GPP flux toward α-terpineol biosynthesis
Endogenous Erg20 in yeast converts GPP to FPP, which limits α-terpineol production. To maximize α-terpineol production, we targeted deletion of the endogenous ERG20 gene. We integrated the ERG20 F96W/N127W and tVvT SM522K/13aa fusion protein into the ERG20 locus of S. cerevisiae WB08, achieving endogenous ERG20 knockout and constructing strain WB09 ( Fig. 4 A). An alternative strategy was also developed: a mitochondrial-targeted ERG20 F96W/N127W and tVvTS M522K/13aa fusion construct was used to knock out endogenous ERG20, generating strain WB10 ( Fig. 4 A). Fermentation results demonstrated that both WB09 and WB10 (with endogenous ERG20 knocked out) exhibited decreased α-terpineol titer and impaired cell growth ( Fig. 4 B). This was likely because reduced intracellular FPP synthesis lowered ergosterol levels (a downstream product of FPP) [ 31 , 32 ]. To mitigate this, we exogenously supplemented 20 mg/L ergosterol into the fermentation medium. While this significantly improved the growth of α-terpineol-producing strains, α-terpineol titer remained notably low ( Fig. 4 C). Insufficient α-terpineol synthase expression emerged as a potential bottleneck. We hypothesized that increasing its gene copy number to boost expression would redirect metabolic flux toward α-terpineol biosynthesis and improve titer.

### 3.4. Enhancing tolerance and mitigating growth-production trade-offs via diploid engineering
α-Terpineol possesses potent antibacterial activity, and its intracellular accumulation can induce significant cytotoxicity even at relatively low titers [ 33 ]. To mitigate α-terpineol toxicity, we selected seven endogenous S. cerevisiae tolerance-associated genes for overexpression screening ( Table S1 ). The candidates were obtained by combining NCBI/database annotations with literature survey. The selection rationale encompassed three protective dimensions: (1) canonical multidrug ABC transporters for extracellular efflux (Pdr5) and vacuolar transporter (Ycf1) of lipophilic xenobiotics [ 34 , 35 ]; (2) mitochondrial membrane transporters and structural components (Atm1, Mic12, Mmr1) to potentially alleviate local toxicity and membrane stress caused by our mitochondrial compartmentalization strategy [ [36] , [37] , [38] ]; and (3) putative stress-responsive clearance proteins (Mga2, Ups1) to evaluate the mitigation of terpene-induced proteotoxic stress [ 39 , 40 ]. These seven candidates were identified and integrated into the HO locus of strain WB02 ( Table S1 ). Among the candidates, overexpression of the ABC transporter Pdr5 yielded the most significant improvement, increasing the α-terpineol titer by 1.22-fold compared to the control ( Fig. 5 A). Notably, compared to the parental strain WB02, all strains overexpressing the tested tolerance-related genes, particularly Pdr5, exhibited improved cell growth. This suggests that even at low production titers, the metabolic burden or inherent cytotoxicity of pathway intermediates can subtly impair cell fitness, and overexpression of tolerance-associated genes overexpression alleviates this stress, thereby promoting better growth. PDR5 is known to enhance β-carotene efflux and improve β-carotene tolerance in S. cerevisiae [ 41 ], and its overexpression may alleviate terpene-associated stress by reducing intracellular toxicity, either through direct export of α-terpineol or through broader detoxification-related effec

### 3.5. Medium optimization and fed-batch fermentation boost α-terpineol titer
Culture medium components affect α-terpineol biosynthesis, and medium optimization is a routine approach to boosting biosynthetic titers [ 42 ]. Key parameters for optimization include adjusting the carbon-to-nitrogen (C/N) ratio and initial pH. Additionally, the α-terpineol synthase used in this study harbors magnesium ion-binding motifs, and the volume fraction of organic extractant also impacts α-terpineol titer. We thus optimized four parameters for WB11 (the highest-titer strain): C/N ratio, Mg 2+ concentration, organic extractant volume fraction, and initial pH. A uniform design using DPS software was used to develop the medium optimization protocol for WB11 ( Table S2 ). The experimental results demonstrated that a C/N ratio of 7:1, pH 6.4, combined with 10 mM Mg 2+ and 25% (v/v) organic phase, yielded the maximum α-terpineol titer of 28.83 ± 2.94 mg/L ( Fig. 6 A). This condition provided an optimal balance between cell growth and terpene synthesis, serving as the basis for the subsequent fed-batch fermentation.

### 4. Discussion
Synthetic biology has enabled the production of various plant-derived monoterpenoids in S. cerevisiae [ 18 , 43 , 44 ]; however, titers for α-terpineol have historically lagged behind those of other terpenes such as limonene and linalool [ 18 , 43 ]. This discrepancy is largely attributed to the complex cyclization mechanism of α-terpineol synthase and the strict regulation of the precursor GPP branch point [ 10 ]. In this study, we established a combinatorial engineering framework addressing three synergistic bottlenecks: catalytic inefficiency, precursor diversion, and cellular toxicity. The resulting strain, WB11, achieved a titer of 81.78 mg/L in a 5-L bioreactor, representing a 1635.6-fold improvement over the initial strain.
In nature, monoterpenoids are predominantly synthesized in plant plastids, and monoterpene synthases typically harbor a plastid-targeting transit peptide at their N-terminus [ 45 ]. Previous studies have demonstrated that truncation of the transit peptide of VvTS is indispensable for its catalytic activity in S. cerevisiae [ 10 ]. Building upon this prior truncation strategy, we further identified redundant sequences within the tVvTS. Subsequent truncation experiments on tVvTS revealed that removing an additional 13 N-terminal amino acids resulted in a two-fold increase in α-terpineol production, representing the best-performing truncation variant under the tested conditions. Notably, truncation of 15 amino acids resulted in an undetectable level of α-terpineol production. We hypothesize that residues 13-15 are located near a structurally important boundary between the flexible N-terminus and the catalytic core. Excessive truncation (i.e., 15 amino acids) is postulated to disrupt the conformational integrity of the catalytic core, thereby abolishing detectable whole-cell production [ 46 ]. This abrupt loss of activity suggests that residues 13–15 may be important for maintaining the structural integrity of the catalytic region. This observ
